extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students studying probability / stochastic processes (Markov chains and random walks)
extracted.subtask_description: Reading and applying textbook results about discrete-time Markov chains and random walks: definitions, key theorems (Markov/strong Markov, recurrence/transience, Chapman–Kolmogorov), and criteria (Lyapunov, Fourier/Chung–Fuchs) used to decide long-term behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markov property / transition probability (Theorem 5.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: X_n is a Markov chain (w.r.t. F_n = σ(X_0, ..., X_n)) with transition probability p; i.e. P_µ(X_{n+1} ∈ B | F_n) = p(X_n, B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by integrating over path-cylinder sets and using π–λ and monotone-class arguments; equivalently for bounded measurable f, E(f(X_{n+1}) | F_n) = ∫ p(X_n, dy) f(y).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-step conditional expectation identity (5.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n has transition probability p then for any bounded measurable f, E(f(X_{n+1}) | F_n) = ∫ p(X_n, dy) f(y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a direct consequence of the Markov property (Theorem 5.2.1) and is used repeatedly to compute conditional expectations and to iterate expectations via transition kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone class theorem for function collections (Theorem 5.2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let A be a π-system containing Ω. Let H be collection of real-valued functions satisfying: (i) 1_A ∈ H for A ∈ A; (ii) closed under addition and scalar multiplication; (iii) closed under increasing limits of nonnegative bounded functions. Then H contains all bounded functions measurable w.r.t. σ(A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to extend identities proved for simple / factorized functions to all bounded measurable functions; standard π–λ + monotone-class style extension device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markov property for path shifts (Theorem 5.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For bounded measurable Y defined on path space and integer m, E_µ(Y ∘ θ_m | F_m) = E_{X_m} Y (i.e., conditional expectation of a future functional given F_m depends on the present state X_m via the law starting from that state).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved first for product cylinder functions then extended by π–λ and monotone-class theorems; the right-hand side is the function φ(x)=E_x Y evaluated at x=X_m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chapman–Kolmogorov equation (Theorem 5.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For transition probabilities, p^{(m+n)}(x,z) = ∑_y p^{(m)}(x,y) p^{(n)}(y,z) (Px(X_{m+n}=z) = ∑_y Px(X_m=y) P_y(X_n=z)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: to go from x to z in m+n steps, must be at some y at time m; deduced from Markov property and law of total probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stopping time σ-algebra and random shift θ_N (definitions before Theorem 5.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: N is a stopping time if {N = n} ∈ F_n. Define F_N = {A : A ∩ {N=n} ∈ F_n for all n} and the shifted path θ_Nω = θ_n ω on {N=n} (with a cemetery point for N=∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These definitions set up the filtration and shift needed to state and apply the strong Markov property at random times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong Markov property (Theorem 5.2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (Y_n) are measurable bounded functions, then E_µ(Y_N ∘ θ_N | F_N) = E_{X_N} Y_N on {N < ∞}, where the right side is ϕ(x,n)=E_x Y_n evaluated at x = X_N, n = N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces to conditioning on {N=n} and applying the ordinary Markov property at deterministic times; standard technique: break down by value of N and reassemble using F_N measurability.

rubrics_metrics.name: k-th return probability factorization (Theorem 5.2.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: For return times T_y^k (time of k-th return to y), Px(T_y^k < ∞) = ρ_{xy} ρ_{yy}^{k-1}, where ρ_{xy} = P_x(T_y < ∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intuition: reach y once (ρ_{xy}) and then need k−1 further returns; derived using strong Markov property and induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection principle for symmetric i.i.d. increments (Theorem 5.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ξ_i are i.i.d. symmetric about 0 and S_n = ∑ ξ_i, then for a > 0: P( max_{m ≤ n} S_m ≥ a ) ≤ 2 P(S_n ≥ a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses stopping time N = inf{m ≤ n : S_m > a}, constructs indicator-function functionals and applies strong Markov property; gives useful bound for maxima in symmetric random walks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional independence of past and future given present (Exercise 5.2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For A ∈ σ(X_0,...,X_n) and B ∈ σ(X_n,X_{n+1},...), P_µ(A ∩ B | X_n) = P_µ(A | X_n) P_µ(B | X_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express left side as nested conditional expectations and apply the Markov property; formalizes that past and future are independent given present state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absorbing state (definition / Exercise 5.2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: State a is absorbing if P_a(X_1 = a) = 1. For D = {X_n = a for some n ≥ 1} and h(x)=P_x(D), one can show h(X_n) → 0 almost surely on D^c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absorbing states are examples of closed sets; hitting probabilities and martingale / limit arguments give asymptotic behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-entrance decomposition of transition probabilities (Exercise 5.2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Ty = inf{n ≥ 1 : X_n = y}, p_n(x,y) = ∑_{m=1}^n P_x(T_y = m) p_{n-m}(y,y).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decomposes n-step transition into the time of first arrival to y and the remainder; useful in studying hitting and return distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exit-distribution harmonic equation and uniqueness (Exercise 5.2.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V_C = inf{n ≥ 0 : X_n ∈ C} and h(x) = P_x(V_A < V_B) for disjoint A,B with S − (A ∪ B) finite and positive hitting probabilities; then for x ∉ A∪B, h(x) = ∑_y p(x,y) h(y). The boundary conditions are h=1 on A and h=0 on B; this solution is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows harmonic (mean-value) property for exit probabilities; uniqueness follows from martingale property of h(X_{n ∧ V_{A∪B}}) and finiteness assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected hitting time solves Poisson-type equation (Exercise 5.2.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: For V_A = inf{n ≥ 0 : X_n ∈ A}, g(x) = E_x V_A solves g(x) = 1 + ∑_y p(x,y) g(y) for x ∉ A, with g=0 on A; under finiteness and positivity assumptions this solution is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: g(X_{n ∧ V_A}) + (n ∧ V_A) is a martingale; uniqueness follows from optional stopping and finiteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: recurrent vs. transient state (start of §5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: State y is recurrent if ρ_{yy} = P_y(T_y < ∞) = 1, and transient if ρ_{yy} < 1. If y is recurrent then P_y(X_n = y i.o.) = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, recurrence means infinite returns with probability 1; transience implies expected number of positive-time visits finite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mean number of visits characterizes recurrence (Theorem 5.3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: y is recurrent iff E_y N(y) = ∞, where N(y) = ∑_{n≥1} 1(X_n = y). For transient y, E_x N(y) = ρ_{xy} / (1 − ρ_{yy}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses geometric series decomposition of return probabilities and the product formula from Theorem 5.2.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagiousness of recurrence (Theorem 5.3.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If x is recurrent and ρ_{xy} > 0 then y is recurrent and ρ_{yx} = 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses reachability and simple path concatenation: if ρ_{xy} > 0 and ρ_{yx} < 1 then ρ_{xx} < 1 contradicting recurrence; also shows propagation of recurrence within communicating classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closed and irreducible sets; finite closed set contains a recurrent state (Theorem 5.3.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: C is closed if x ∈ C and ρ_{xy} > 0 implies y ∈ C. If C is finite and closed then C contains at least one recurrent state; if C is irreducible (every pair communicates) then all states in C are recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses contradiction via summing expected visits over finite closed set; identifies recurrent classes in finite-state chains by graph/communication structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of recurrent states into closed irreducible components (Theorem 5.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let R = {x : ρ_{xx} = 1} be the recurrent states. Then R = ⋃_i R_i where each R_i is closed and irreducible (the sets C_x = {y : ρ_{xy} > 0} partition R into closed irreducible components).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reduces study of recurrence to studying single irreducible closed classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lyapunov / supermartingale criterion for recurrence (Theorem 5.3.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is irreducible and there exists ϕ ≥ 0 with E_x ϕ(X_1) ≤ ϕ(x) for x ∉ F (a finite set) and ϕ(x) → ∞ as x → ∞ (i.e., level sets {x: ϕ(x) ≤ M} are finite), then the chain is recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: ϕ(X_{n ∧ τ}) is a supermartingale for τ = hitting time of F; use optional stopping and irreducibility to show positive recurrence of all states in effect, hence recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birth-and-death chain potential function and hitting probabilities (Theorems 5.3.10 & 5.3.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define ϕ by ϕ(0)=0, ϕ(1)=1 and for k≥1 differences ϕ(k+1)−ϕ(k) = ∏_{j=1}^k (q_j / p_j). Then for a < x < b, P_x(T_a < T_b) = (ϕ(b) − ϕ(x)) / (ϕ(b) − ϕ(a)). Moreover 0 is recurrent iff ϕ(∞) = ∑_{m=0}^∞ ∏_{j=1}^m (q_j / p_j) = ∞; if finite, P_x(T_0 = ∞) = ϕ(x) / ϕ(∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ϕ(X_{n ∧ T}) is a martingale; typical technique to reduce hitting probabilities and recurrence to series / product conditions on transition ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random-walk recurrent-value subgroup criterion (Theorem 5.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a random walk S_n in R^d, the set V of recurrent values is either empty or a closed subgroup of R^d; in the latter case V equals U, the set of possible values (points that the walk can hit with positive probability at some time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key step: if x ∈ U and y ∈ V then y − x ∈ V; closure and group properties follow; reduces recurrence questions to structure of reachable subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent return-time criteria for recurrence of random walk (Theorem 5.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For random walk S_n, the following are equivalent: (i) P(τ_1 < ∞) = 1 (first return time), (ii) P(S_n = 0 i.o.) = 1, (iii) ∑_{m=0}^∞ P(S_m = 0) = ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses renewal-type decomposition of visits to 0 and geometric nature of successive return probabilities; links almost-sure event to divergence of expected counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polya's theorem for simple random walk (Theorem 5.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple symmetric random walk on Z^d is recurrent for d ≤ 2 and transient for d ≥ 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1D: asymptotics ρ_1(2n) ~ (π n)^{-1/2}; 2D: ρ_2(2n) = ρ_1(2n)^2 ~ (π n)^{-1}; 3D+: higher-dimensional combinatorial bounds and Stirling estimates show summability of return probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borel–Cantelli sum criterion for recurrence/transience (Lemmas 5.4.5, 5.4.6 and Theorem 5.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ∑_n P(||S_n|| < δ) < ∞ then P(||S_n|| < δ i.o.) = 0 (transient). If ∑_n P(||S_n|| < δ) = ∞ then P(||S_n|| < 2δ i.o.) = 1 (recurrent). The divergence/convergence for one δ > 0 suffices to classify recurrence/transience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Borel–Cantelli and an independence/renewal argument plus a covering/counting lemma (Lemma 5.4.6) to show the property is robust to scaling of δ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chung–Fuchs criterion in one dimension (Theorem 5.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If d=1 and S_n / n → 0 in probability (weak law of large numbers form), then the random walk is recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lemma 5.4.6 to relate probabilities at different scales and average arguments to deduce divergence of ∑ P(|S_n|<1) and then Theorem 5.4.7.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-dimensional CLT criterion (Theorem 5.4.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S_n is a random walk in R^2 and S_n / √n ⇒ a nondegenerate normal distribution, then S_n is recurrent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local limit behaviour yields that P(||S_n|| < m) behaves like density times area; integrate and use Lemma 5.4.6 and divergence arguments to show ∑ P(||S_n||<1) = ∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fourier / characteristic-function recurrence criterion (Theorems 5.4.10 & 5.4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let φ(t) = E e^{i t·X_1} be one-step ch.f. Then recurrence is equivalent to (for some δ>0) ∫_{(-δ,δ)^d} Re(1 / (1 − φ(y))) dy = ∞. A proved weaker form: ∫_{(-δ,δ)^d} sup_{r<1} Re(1/(1 − r φ(y))) dy = ∞ iff recurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Parseval relation (Lemma 5.4.12), analytic bounds on trigonometric terms (Lemma 5.4.13), smoothing kernels and dominated convergence / Fatou arguments; this gives an analytic test for recurrence in terms of behavior of φ near 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parseval relation for characteristic functions (Lemma 5.4.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For probability measures µ and ν with ch.f.'s ϕ and ψ, ∫ ψ(t) µ(dt) = ∫ ϕ(x) ν(dx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to relate probabilities (or densities) of sums to integrals of characteristic functions; justification by Fubini since e^{i t·x} is bounded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trigonometric lower bound (Lemma 5.4.13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For |x| ≤ π/3, 1 − cos x ≥ x^2 / 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elementary calculus inequality used to derive lower bounds for Fourier kernels and control integrands in the Fourier recurrence criterion.
